requirement: # Requirement: Set Collection Primitive  **ID:** REQ-SET-001 **Title:** Implement a `Set` primitive as a first-class collection type, complementary to the existing `Dictionary` and `Array` primitives **Status:** Draft for implementation  ---  ## 1. Motivation  The runtime currently provides `Array` (ordered, indexable sequence) and `Dictionary` (unordered key→value mapping) as its only built-in collection types. There is no dedicated primitive for representing an unordered collection of unique elements. Users are forced to emulate sets with `Array` + linear `contains` scans (O(n) membership) or with `Dictionary` using dummy values (exposing meaningless keys/values through the public API).  A first-class `Set` primitive removes these workarounds, enables O(1) average membership testing, provides standard set algebra, and makes intent explicit in user code and in the type signatures of standard-library functions.  ---  ## 2. Scope  ### 2.1 In scope - A new built-in `Set` value type, implemented in the runtime core (not as a user-space library), with parity in native support, GC integration, and interop with `Array`/`Dictionary`. - Creation, mutation, and inspection operations. - Set algebra (union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference) and relation predicates. - Element hashing/equality rules consistent with those used by `Dictionary` keys. - Functional operations (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`) that return the appropriate collection type. - Conversion to and from `Array` and `Dictionary`. - Literal and constructor syntax. - Serialization/deserialization support in the standard JSON/text codecs. - Interop rules with `Array` and `Dictionary` (membership testing, equality comparison, spread/iteration). - Documentation and language reference updates.  ### 2.2 Out of scope - Ordered/sorted sets, multi-sets (bags), and set-with-expiry. - Mutable keys, thread-safety guarantees beyond the runtime's existing synchronization model for `Dictionary`/`Array`. - New hash algorithms; `Set` must reuse the runtime's existing hash/equality implementation.  ---  ## 3. Functional Requirements  ### 3.1 Construction | Requirement | Detail | |---|---| | FR-1.1 | `Set()` creates an empty set. | | FR-1.2 | `Set(iterable)` creates a set from any iterable whose elements are hashable; duplicate elements are collapsed, keeping the first occurrence. | | FR-1.3 | `Set(arrayLike)` must accept `Array` and any other iterable, and must accept another `Set` (producing an independent copy). | | FR-1.4 | A literal form (e.g. `#{a, b, c}`, syntax to match host-language conventions) desugars to `Set` construction with constant-folded contents. An empty literal yields an empty set. | | FR-1.5 | `Set` values are value-like with copy-on-write semantics: assigning a set to a variable or inserting it into a container must not allow aliasing to mutate both. |  ### 3.2 Core operations | ID | Operation | Contract | |---|---|---| | FR-2.1 | `add(element)` | Inserts `element` if absent. Returns `true` if the element was added, `false` if it was already present. No-op on duplicates. | | FR-2.2 | `remove(element)` | Removes `element` if present; returns `true` if removed, `false` otherwise. | | FR-2.3 | `discard(element)` | Removes `element` if present, otherwise does nothing; never raises for missing elements. | | FR-2.4 | `contains(element)` | Returns `true` if `element` is a member. Average O(1). | | FR-2.5 | `size` / `count` | Number of distinct elements; O(1). | | FR-2.6 | `isEmpty` | `true` when the set has no elements. | | FR-2.7 | `clear()` | Removes all elements; sets `size` to 0. | | FR-2.8 | `copy()` | Returns an independent shallow copy of the set. | | FR-2.9 | `toArray()` | Returns an `Array` of the elements. Order must be documented (see §4.3). | | FR-2.10 | `toDictionary()` | Returns a `Dictionary` mapping each element to `true` (or the documented sentinel), enabling idiomatic value lookups. | | FR-2.11 | `union(other)` / `intersection(other)` / `difference(other)` / `symmetricDifference(other)` | Return a **new** `Set`; operands are not mutated. `other` may be a `Set` or any iterable. | | FR-2.12 | `isSubsetOf(other)` / `isSupersetOf(other)` / `isDisjointWith(other)` / `isEqualTo(other)` | Return booleans. | | FR-2.13 | `map(fn)` | Returns an `Array` of `fn` applied to each element. | | FR-2.14 | `filter(predicate)` | Returns a new `Set` of elements satisfying `predicate`. | | FR-2.15 | `reduce(initial, fn)` | Left fold over elements in iteration order; returns the accumulator. | | FR-2.16 | `forEach(fn)` | Invokes `fn(element)` once per element in iteration order. | | FR-2.17 | `pop()`/`removeFirst()` (if the host `Array` exposes such mutators) | Removes and returns an arbitrary element, or `nil`/`null` when empty — semantics and naming must match the existing `Array`/`Dictionary` mutator conventions. |  ### 3.3 Interop and language integration - **FR-3.1** `element in someSet` and `someSet contains element` are both supported and equivalent. - **FR-3.2** `Set` is iterable (usable in `for` loops and spread into `Set(...)`, `Array(...)`). - **FR-3.3** Set algebra is also expressible via operator syntax where the language supports operator overloading (e.g. `|`, `&`, `-`, `^`), and these operators must have the same semantics as the named methods. - **FR-3.4** Equality: two sets are equal iff they contain the same elements, regardless of insertion order. - **FR-3.5** `Set` participates in `==`/`!=` comparison with `Array`/`Dictionary` by returning `false` (no cross-type coercion), except that `Set` vs. `Set` uses set equality. - **FR-3.6** A `Set` may be used as a `Dictionary` key only if the set is immutable/frozen per the runtime's existing rules for hashable keys; the runtime must produce a documented, deterministic error otherwise. - **FR-3.7** Standard-library functions that accept "any iterable collection" (e.g. `join`, `flatten`, `unique`, `groupBy`) must accept `Set` without modification. - **FR-3.8** A `unique()` (or equivalent) helper on `Array` should be implementable by delegating to `Set` internally.  ### 3.4 Error handling | ID | Condition | Required behavior | |---|---|---| | FR-4.1 | Element is unhashable (e.g. an `Array`, `Dictionary`, function, or other non-hashable value) | Raise the runtime's standard type error (`TypeError`), naming `Set` and the offending type. Must not crash the process or corrupt the set. | | FR-4.2 | Operation receives a non-iterable argument where an iterable is required | Raise the standard type error. | | FR-4.3 | `remove` on an absent element | Must not raise; return `false` (per FR-2.2). If the host convention requires `remove` to raise on missing keys (as `Dictionary.remove` may), `Set.remove` must match that convention and the behavior must be documented and tested. | | FR-4.4 | Errors raised during iteration (e.g. element mutated during `forEach`) | Must follow the runtime's existing invalidation semantics for `Dictionary`/`Array`. |  ---  ## 4. Non-Functional Requirements  ### 4.1 Performance - **NFR-1.1** `contains`, `add`, `remove` must be O(1) average time, using the same hashing strategy and open-addressing/chaining design as `Dictionary`. - **NFR-1.2** `add` of an existing element must be O(1) and must not grow the backing storage. - **NFR-1.3** Set algebra operations must be O(n + m) in the sizes of the operands. - **NFR-1.4** `Set` must not be more than 2× the memory footprint of an equivalent `Dictionary` with the same elements.  ### 4.2 Correctness and consistency - **NFR-2.1** Hash/equality semantics for elements must be identical to `Dictionary` key semantics: `a == b` ⇒ `hash(a) == hash(b)`, and elements that compare equal are treated as the same member. - **NFR-2.2** The implementation must pass the runtime's existing conformance suite for collections plus a new dedicated `Set` test suite. - **NFR-2.3** No regressions in `Array`/`Dictionary` performance or behavior (benchmark suite must show no statistically significant regression).  ### 4.3 Determinism - **NFR-3.1** Iteration order must be deterministic and documented: either insertion order is preserved, or a stable but unspecified order derived from the hash table is used. The chosen order must be stable across runs for the same insertion sequence and must not change when an unrelated element is added or removed (if hash-order is chosen, removal-induced rehash effects must not reorder unaffected elements — e.g. use tombstones rather than re-inserting).  ### 4.4 Serialization - **NFR-4.1** JSON/text encoders must encode `Set` as a JSON array of its elements in iteration order. - **NFR-4.2** Decoders must accept a JSON array and produce a `Set`, collapsing duplicates. - **NFR-4.3** Round-trip encode→decode must yield an equal set.  ### 4.5 Portability and API stability - **NFR-5.1** `Set` must be implemented in the runtime core with the same cross-platform support matrix as `Array`/`Dictionary` (all supported architectures/interpreters). - **NFR-5.2** The public API must be documented in the language reference, and the feature must be covered by a versioned API-stability note.  ---  ## 5. Acceptance Criteria  1. `Set` is a built-in type constructible via `Set()`, `Set(iterable)`, and literal syntax, with no imports required. 2. All operations in §3.2 are implemented, behave as specified, and are covered by unit tests — including edge cases: empty set, single element, duplicate insertion, removal of absent element, self-union/intersection/difference, `difference` with a superset, symmetric difference, sets of mixed element types, and sets containing `nil`/`null` (if `nil` is hashable in the host language). 3. `contains` returns `true`/`false` exactly for members; membership is consistent with `Dictionary` key lookup for the same element. 4. Attempting to add an unhashable element raises a `TypeError` with a clear message and leaves the set unmodified. 5. Set equality is order-independent; `Set([1,2]) == Set([2,1])` is `true`. 6. `Array`/`Dictionary`/spread/`for` iteration over a `Set` works, and existing standard-library collection functions accept `Set` arguments. 7. JSON round-trip of a `Set` preserves its contents. 8. Benchmarks show `contains` on a 100k-element set is at least 100× faster than the equivalent linear `Array` scan. 9. The full existing test suite passes with no regressions; new `Set` tests achieve full coverage of the added code paths. 10. Documentation (language reference + standard-library API docs) is updated, including element hashability rules, iteration-order guarantees, and error behavior.  ---  ## 6. Deliverables  - Core `Set` type implementation (runtime + GC/ownership integration). - Built-in constructor, literal syntax, and parser/desugaring support. - Interop with `Array`, `Dictionary`, iterators, and operator syntax. - JSON/text (de)serialization support. - Unit, conformance, and property-based tests (e.g. algebraic laws: `A ∪ B = B ∪ A`, `A ∩ B ⊆ A`, `A \ A = ∅`, `A △ A = ∅`, De Morgan identities). - Benchmarks comparing `Set` vs. `Array`-based emulation. - Language reference and API documentation updates.
explanation: The requirement is extensively detailed with explicit contracts, making it largely unambiguous; only a few points (e.g., iteration order, literal syntax) leave room for interpretation. It provides measurable criteria (O(1) operations, benchmarks, test cases) and clear acceptance criteria, so it is highly verifiable. However, it encompasses many distinct capabilities (construction, core operations, algebra, interop, serialization, etc.), which means it is not a single, focused requirement, resulting in a low singularity score.

requirement: ## Requirement: Include images in rustdoc output Rustdoc shall support images referenced in crate-level, module-level, and item-level documentation and include them in generated HTML documentation. ### Functional requirements - Standard Markdown image syntax (`![alt text](url "optional title")`) shall be recognized in doc comments and in Markdown included through `#![doc = include_str!("...")]`. - Each recognized image shall produce an HTML `` element containing the resolved `src`, an `alt` attribute, and a `title` attribute when one is provided. - Remote image URLs, including HTTP and HTTPS URLs, shall be preserved and referenced directly. - Relative image paths shall be resolved against the source document, validated during documentation generation, and copied into the generated documentation output. The copied asset shall not depend on files remaining in the source tree. - Generated asset paths shall avoid collisions and shall not reference locations outside the documentation output directory. - Missing or unreadable image files shall produce a diagnostic identifying the documentation source and image path; images shall not be silently omitted. - Existing Markdown rendering, HTML sanitization, link resolution, and non-HTML rustdoc output shall remain backward compatible. ### Acceptance criteria - A doc comment containing `![Architecture](images/architecture.png)` generates an `` element with `alt="Architecture"`, and the referenced file is available in the generated output. - A crate-level document loaded with `include_str!` renders both local and remote Markdown images correctly. - A broken local image path reports the source document and missing path while allowing rustdoc to continue generating documentation.
explanation: The requirement is mostly clear and precise, defining exact syntax and expected HTML output, though a few statements (e.g., collision avoidance) are somewhat open to interpretation. It offers concrete, testable conditions (e.g., presence, diagnostics) that can be verified by examining generated documentation and error messages. However, it bundles many distinct capabilities (syntax recognition, HTML generation, asset copying, error handling, backward compatibility), making it non‑singular.

requirement: ### Requirement: MPS Operator Coverage Tracking  The project shall maintain a centralized tracker documenting operator coverage for the MPS backend. For every operator in the project’s supported operator set, the tracker must record:  - Support status: **Supported**, **Partial**, **Unsupported**, or **Not Applicable**. - Relevant MPS version, device, dtype, shape, and model constraints. - Implementation path, including native MPS kernels, fallback mechanisms, or planned work. - Validation status and links to automated or manual tests. - Known limitations, workarounds, and issue ownership.  Support may be marked **Supported** only when the operator passes the project’s parity tests against the reference backend. Any change that adds, removes, or modifies MPS operator support, limitations, or tests must update the tracker in the same change. CI must detect missing tracker entries, stale coverage claims, and regressions in supported operators. The tracker must provide an aggregate coverage summary and identify remaining coverage gaps for prioritization.
explanation: The requirement is precise and detailed, enumerates clear statuses and fields, ties support to verifiable parity tests and CI checks, and defines a single centralized tracker responsibility, resulting in high unambiguity, verifiability, and singularity.

requirement: # Requirement: Run `compute()` on a Separate Thread (Web Worker) in Flutter Web  ## 1. Background / Problem  `compute()` from `package:flutter/foundation.dart` is the canonical way for Flutter applications to offload CPU-bound work (e.g. JSON parsing, image processing, encryption) off the UI thread by executing it in a background isolate. On mobile and desktop targets this is implemented with `dart:isolate` and executes on a genuinely separate OS thread.  On the web, there is no OS thread model and `dart:isolate`'s `Isolate.spawn` is unsupported. The current web implementation of `compute()` executes the supplied callback **inline on the main UI thread** (or otherwise degrades to synchronous execution), so:  - Long-running callbacks **block rendering and input handling**, causing visible jank/frozen frames. - Developers get no performance benefit from `compute()` on web, and cross-platform code that relies on `compute()` for responsiveness silently regresses. - Platform behavior is inconsistent: the same source code behaves differently on web vs. native, which is a correctness and API-parity defect.  ## 2. Goal  Make `compute()` (and the isolate-style background execution API surface exposed by `package:flutter`) execute the caller's callback on a **separate thread** in Flutter Web by leveraging **Web Workers**, preserving the same semantics, error reporting, and API contract as the native (IO) implementation.  ## 3. Scope  **In scope**  - `package:flutter/foundation.dart` → `compute()` on web targets. - The underlying isolate/worker abstraction used by the framework (worker creation, message passing, termination, error propagation). - Support for all Flutter web compilation modes (debug, profile, release, `dart2js` and `dart2wasm`/WasmGC builds). - Framework-side documentation and changelog updates, plus public-API documentation clarifying web behavior.  **Out of scope**  - Adding general-purpose `dart:isolate` support to the Dart web SDK (this requirement consumes worker-based background execution; a full `dart:isolate` web implementation is a separate SDK-level effort). - Unstructured concurrency (`Isolate.run` with arbitrary closures/async gaps) unless it can be supported without breaking existing web semantics. - GPU/OffscreenCanvas-based compute offload. - Changes to native (IO) behavior.  ## 4. Functional Requirements  ### FR-1 — True off-thread execution - `compute<T, R>(ComputeCallback<T, R> callback, T message)` on web MUST execute `callback` inside a Web Worker (a dedicated background thread), never on the main UI thread. - The main thread MUST remain responsive (able to process frames and input events) while the callback is running.  ### FR-2 — API and semantic parity with native - The web implementation MUST match the native contract for:   - Calling `callback` exactly once per `compute()` invocation.   - Completing the returned `Future<R>` exactly once with the callback's return value.   - Propagating errors thrown by the callback to the caller. - `compute()` MUST remain usable without any web-specific API changes at call sites; existing code must not require modification to gain the benefit.  ### FR-3 — Message and result serialization - The `message` argument and the callback's return value MUST be transferable between the main thread and the worker. - Supported types MUST include, at minimum: `null`, `bool`, `int`, `double`, `String`, `List`, `Map`, `Set`, `Uint8List`, and other `TypedData`/`TransferableTypedData` types. - Types that cannot be transferred (e.g. arbitrary class instances, closures, `ReceivePort`s) MUST produce a clear, actionable error consistent with the native implementation's "not sendable" error behavior — the operation MUST NOT hang and MUST NOT silently produce a wrong result.  ### FR-4 — Error propagation - An uncaught exception thrown inside the worker MUST be surfaced to the `compute()` caller as an error with:   - The original error message and type where available.   - The original stack trace (or the worker-side stack trace) preserved in the resulting error's `stackTrace`. - Errors MUST be distinguishable from transport/protocol failures.  ### FR-5 — Worker lifecycle and resource management - Worker startup MUST be amortized: the framework SHOULD reuse a worker (or a small pool of workers) across `compute()` calls rather than paying full worker instantiation cost on every call, while still guaranteeing that a single `compute()` invocation runs in exactly one worker context. - Workers MUST be terminated and their resources released when no longer needed, and MUST NOT accumulate indefinitely over the application's lifetime. - Terminating or tearing down a worker MUST NOT leave the caller's `Future` unresolved; pending futures MUST be completed with an error.  ### FR-6 — Graceful degradation / unsupported environments - If the environment cannot create a Web Worker (e.g. blocked by a Content Security Policy that disallows `worker-src`/`blob:` workers, or a non-browser host), `compute()` MUST either:   - fall back to synchronous inline execution with a documented, debug-visible warning, or   - fail with a descriptive `UnsupportedError` naming the cause,   and the chosen behavior MUST be consistent and documented. - The fallback path MUST be surfaced in debug builds (e.g. via `debugPrint`/assertion) so developers are not misled into believing off-thread execution occurred.  ### FR-7 — Build-mode and tooling compatibility - The implementation MUST work in debug, profile, and release web builds, and with both `dart2js` and `dart2wasm` compilation targets. - The worker bootstrap code MUST be bundled/emitted correctly by the web toolchain (including code-splitting/route-based lazy builds) and MUST NOT require the application author to add extra files, `web/` directory entries, or asset declarations to their project. - Worker source maps SHOULD be preserved in debug/profile builds.  ### FR-8 — Observability and diagnostics - Debug builds SHOULD provide a way to observe worker creation, reuse, execution time, and termination (e.g. verbose logging behind a flag), to aid performance analysis.  ## 5. Non-Functional Requirements  | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | NFR-1 | Main-thread blocking time attributable to `compute()` invocation overhead MUST be bounded and small relative to the work offloaded; overhead MUST be measured and published. | | NFR-2 | No measurable regression in startup time, rendering performance, or memory footprint for applications that do not use `compute()`. | | NFR-3 | Thread safety: no shared mutable state between main thread and worker; all communication via message passing with the documented type allow-list. | | NFR-4 | Security: workers MUST be same-origin and MUST NOT use `eval`-based workarounds that would violate a strict CSP without an explicit, documented opt-in. | | NFR-5 | Compatibility with the officially supported browser matrix (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, and mobile equivalents), including browsers where worker startup cost is high. | | NFR-6 | The feature MUST be opt-in-free for callers (no new required API) but MAY be gated internally behind an experimental flag until stabilized. | | NFR-7 | The implementation MUST be testable in the framework's automated test infrastructure (unit, integration, and web-specific browser tests). |  ## 6. Acceptance Criteria  **AC-1 — Off-thread execution** - **Given** a Flutter web app that calls `compute()` with a callback that busy-loops for ~2 seconds, - **When** the callback is running, - **Then** the UI continues to render and respond to input (frame timings show no multi-second stall), and the callback's thread/worker identity differs from the main thread's.  **AC-2 — Result correctness** - **Given** `compute()` with a callback returning a complex serializable structure (nested maps/lists, `Uint8List`), - **When** it completes, - **Then** the returned value is deep-equal to the expected structure and byte-identical for binary payloads.  **AC-3 — Error propagation** - **Given** a callback that throws a custom exception with a message, - **When** `compute()` is awaited, - **Then** the future completes with an error containing the original message and a non-empty stack trace referencing the callback.  **AC-4 — Non-sendable argument** - **Given** `compute()` invoked with an argument that cannot be transferred, - **When** the call is made, - **Then** it fails fast with a descriptive error and does not hang.  **AC-5 — Repeated use / no leaks** - **Given** an app that calls `compute()` 1,000 times sequentially, - **When** the calls complete, - **Then** all futures complete correctly, and the number of live workers remains bounded (reused or pooled), with no unbounded growth in worker count or memory.  **AC-6 — Unsupported environment** - **Given** a page whose CSP forbids worker creation, - **When** `compute()` is invoked, - **Then** the documented fallback or `UnsupportedError` occurs, and a diagnostic is emitted in debug mode.  **AC-7 — Cross-platform parity** - **Given** an identical application source using `compute()`, - **When** built for web and for a native target, - **Then** the observable API behavior (result values, error semantics, call counts) matches.  **AC-8 — Regression safety** - **Given** an application that never calls `compute()`, - **When** built for web, - **Then** bundle size, startup time, and rendering performance are unchanged within the tolerance defined by the web performance benchmarks.  ## 7. Documentation & Communication Requirements  - Update the API documentation for `compute()` to state explicitly that on web the computation runs in a Web Worker (separate thread) and list the transferable/serializable types. - Add a release note / changelog entry describing the new web behavior, including any behavior differences from native. - Publish guidance for developers whose deployments restrict workers (CSP) describing the fallback behavior and required CSP directives. - Provide a migration note for anyone relying on the previous inline-execution behavior on web (e.g. code that depended on synchronous side effects).  ## 8. Open Questions  1. Should `compute()` on web default to a **single shared worker** (serialized execution) or a **worker pool** (parallel execution) when multiple `compute()` calls are in flight concurrently? 2. What is the exact fallback contract when workers are unavailable: silent inline execution with a warning, or a hard `UnsupportedError`? 3. Is `Isolate.run`/`Isolate.spawn`-style API exposure in scope for web in a follow-up, or is `compute()` the sole supported surface? 4. What is the acceptable per-call overhead target for worker message round-trips given worker startup cost on Safari? 5. Should worker usage be made observable via `Timeline`/performance overlay events in debug builds?
explanation: The requirement is detailed and mostly clear, with explicit functional requirements and testable acceptance criteria that support high verifiability. A few design choices (e.g., fallback behavior) are left open, slightly reducing unambiguity, and the specification aggregates many distinct sub‑requirements, so it is not a single‑focused statement.

requirement: ## Requirement: `go mod why` must explain every module in the build list  ### Background  `go list -m all` reports every module in the main module's build list, including modules that are present only because the module graph (MVS) requires them and are never imported. Today, `go mod why` can only produce an import-based explanation, so for many of those modules it has no answer: it either prints an empty/omitted chain, or fails outright with an error such as `module <path>: not a known dependency`, even though the module is listed by `go list -m all`. Users (and tools) therefore cannot tell *why* a given module is in the build list.  ### Required behavior  1. **Complete coverage.** Running `go mod why -m all` must produce exactly one explanation for every module reported by `go list -m all`. The command must not fail, and must not omit or leave blank any module's entry.  2. **Two kinds of explanations.**    - If the module is needed to build packages in the main module (i.e., some package of the module is imported, transitively, by the main module or by one of its dependencies), `go mod why` must print the existing chain of imports/requirements leading from the main module to that package, e.g.:      ```      main/module      main/module/pkg      example.com/needed@v1.2.3      example.com/needed/pkg      ```    - If the module is **not** imported by anything in the main module's import graph, `go mod why` must still answer, using the module requirement graph: it must report the chain of module requirements (`go mod graph` edges) that brings the module into the build list, e.g.:      ```      main/module      example.com/intermediate@v1.0.0      example.com/unused@v1.1.0      ```      or, if no requirement path exists, it must state explicitly that the main module does not need the module and give the reason it is nevertheless in the build list (for example, it is required for the module graph only / by a test-only or indirect dependency).  3. **Per-module queries.** `go mod why -m <module>` for a module that appears in `go list -m all` must return a non-empty explanation of the same form described above (import chain, requirement path, or an explicit "not needed, and here's why it is in the build list" statement). It must not report the module as unknown when it is present in the build list.  4. **Consistency.** The set of modules for which `go mod why` returns an explanation must be identical to the set reported by `go list -m all`; the two commands must agree on the build list and on the selected versions of each module.  5. **Output stability.** The explanation must be deterministic (stable ordering of modules and of the chains) so that the output can be diffed and consumed by tooling.  ### Acceptance criteria  - For a main module whose `go.mod` requires a module that is never imported, `go mod why -m all` lists that module with a requirement-path explanation rather than an empty line or an error. - `go mod why -m all` exits with status 0 and prints one line-block per module in `go list -m all`, with no blank or missing entries. - `go mod why -m <mod>` succeeds for every module in `go list -m all`. - Existing import-chain output for needed modules is preserved (no regression in format or content). - The behavior is covered by `cmd/go` tests (e.g., `script/mod_why.sh`) including a test module with an unimported requirement.
explanation: The requirement is written with precise, unambiguous terminology and includes concrete, testable acceptance criteria, making it highly verifiable. However, it bundles several distinct capabilities (complete coverage, two explanation forms, per‑module queries, consistency, and output stability), so it is not singular.

requirement: # Requirement: Unified Data Reading Framework for PyTorch  ## 1. Title  Unified Data Reading Framework for PyTorch — multi-backend data source access (Hive, MySQL, S3, local filesystem)  ## 2. Motivation  PyTorch training pipelines currently require bespoke, hand-written data loaders per storage backend. Reading from Hive tables, relational databases (MySQL/PostgreSQL), or object stores (S3-compatible) typically means implementing custom `torch.utils.data.Dataset`/`IterableDataset` subclasses, duplicating logic for schema decoding, sharding across ranks, batching, shuffling, caching, credentials handling, and retries for every project. This results in duplicated code, inconsistent behavior across distributed workers, poor failure semantics, and tight coupling of training code to infrastructure details.  A single, declarative data reading framework is required that abstracts storage backends behind a common interface, exposing records to PyTorch as standard `Dataset`/`IterableDataset` objects so that training code remains backend-agnostic.  ## 3. Goals  1. Provide a single, stable Python API for reading training/inference data from heterogeneous backends (Hive, MySQL, S3, local filesystem) with no change to training code when switching backends. 2. Expose read results through standard PyTorch constructs (`torch.utils.data.Dataset`, `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset`, `DataLoader`) including native multi-worker and distributed (DDP/FSDP) support. 3. Support declarative configuration (Python API + YAML/JSON config file) so pipelines are reproducible and versionable. 4. Support distributed-aware sharding, deterministic ordering, and reproducible shuffling across ranks and workers. 5. Support schema inference and type conversion (SQL types ↔ Python types ↔ `torch` dtypes), plus composable record-level transformation pipelines. 6. Support pluggable backends so that new sources can be added without modifying framework core code.  ## 4. Non-Goals (Out of Scope)  - Not a data processing/compute engine (no Spark-like query planning, joins, or aggregation). - Not a replacement for `torch.utils.data.DataLoader`; the framework integrates with it rather than reimplementing it. - Not a feature store, dataset versioning system, or model/data governance platform. - Not a distributed training framework; it must be compatible with existing PyTorch distributed launchers. - Backend-specific advanced features (e.g., Hive ACID transactional semantics, MySQL stored procedures) are out of scope.  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### 5.1 Core Abstraction  - **FR-1.** The framework shall define a `DataSource` abstract base class representing a readable data source, with at minimum:   - `schema` property returning a resolved schema (column name → type, nullable flag);   - `read(...)` / iteration method yielding batches of records;   - `get_reader(config)` returning a configured reader instance. - **FR-2.** The framework shall define a `Reader` interface responsible for producing batches for a given `DataSource`, split/shard specification, and runtime context (rank, world size, worker id). - **FR-3.** The framework shall define a `Backend` plugin interface with methods `open()`, `read_batch(...)`, `close()`, `infer_schema()`, enabling third-party extension by subclassing and registering via an entry point/decorator. - **FR-4.** The framework shall provide a public factory function (e.g., `read(source_spec)` / `build_dataset(spec)`) that returns a `torch.utils.data.Dataset` or `IterableDataset` object based on the source type and configuration. - **FR-5.** All public classes, functions, and configuration keys shall be importable from a single top-level package namespace with stable, documented names and semantic versioning guarantees.  ### 5.2 Backend Connectors  - **FR-6. Hive.** Support reading from Hive tables via ThriftServer/metastore or JDBC. Requirements:   - Column selection and predicate pushdown (partition predicates, WHERE clauses) where supported;   - Partition-aware scanning (e.g., `dt=YYYY-MM-DD`) with partition pruning;   - Schema inference from metastore with explicit type override support;   - Support for ORC/Parquet/sequence-file underlying formats via HiveServer2 or direct object-store access. - **FR-7. MySQL.** Support reading from MySQL tables/views. Requirements:   - Connection pooling with configurable pool size and lifetime;   - Cursor-based streaming reads (server-side unbuffered cursors) to avoid loading full result sets into memory;   - Support for `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT/OFFSET` clauses passed through from configuration;   - Consistent snapshot reads within a single reader instance where isolation level is configurable. - **FR-8. S3.** Support reading from S3 and S3-compatible object stores (MinIO, Ceph, R2). Requirements:   - Prefix/glob-based listing with optional recursive traversal;   - Support for CSV, JSON/JSONL, Parquet, and compressed variants (`.gz`, `.zst`, `.bz2`);   - Support for reading directly via `s3://` URIs in Hive/Hadoop-backed sources. - **FR-9. Local filesystem.** Support reading local files/directories using the same format handling as S3 for parity of behavior. - **FR-10.** Each backend shall be implemented as an independent plugin module; enabling/disabling a backend shall not require modification of framework core code or of other backends. - **FR-11.** Backends requiring optional third-party dependencies shall import them lazily and raise a clear, actionable error (naming the missing package and install command) rather than failing at package import time.  ### 5.3 Schema, Types, and Transformations  - **FR-12.** Schema inference shall be supported for all backends, with the ability to explicitly declare a schema in configuration to override inference. - **FR-13.** A type-mapping layer shall convert backend-native types to Python types and to `torch` dtypes, covering at minimum: integers (signed/unsigned, 8/16/32/64-bit), floats (16/32/64), booleans, strings/bytes, dates, timestamps, and nullable variants. - **FR-14.** Null values shall be represented consistently (e.g., `None`) and shall be convertible to framework-appropriate sentinels (e.g., `NaN`, `0`, or a configurable value) for numeric tensor columns. - **FR-15.** The framework shall provide a composable record-level transformation pipeline: `map`, `filter`, `select/rename`, `cast`, `fill_null`, `shuffle_buffer`, and `batch`. - **FR-16.** Transformations shall be composable in declaration order, and each stage shall be individually testable and inspectable. - **FR-17.** User-defined transformation callables shall receive a structured record/dict and return a dict, or a tensor/batch, and shall support both map-style (indexable) and iterable-style pipelines.  ### 5.4 PyTorch Integration  - **FR-18.** The framework shall return objects that are subclasses of, or fully interoperable with, `torch.utils.data.Dataset` and `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset`. - **FR-19.** Map-style datasets shall support `__len__` and `__getitem__` with configurable index-based or range-based access, including optional in-memory caching of the index metadata (e.g., row offsets) to avoid repeated scans. - **FR-20.** Iterable datasets shall implement `__iter__` yielding individual samples, and be compatible with `DataLoader(batch_size=..., collate_fn=...)`. - **FR-21.** The framework shall not require users to supply a `collate_fn` for common cases; a default collate supporting dict-of-lists and dict-of-tensors shall be provided, with the ability to override. - **FR-22.** Existing user-defined `collate_fn`, `sampler`, and `transform` hooks of `DataLoader` shall continue to work unchanged. - **FR-23.** The framework shall support `torch.utils.data.DataLoader` with `num_workers > 0`, including correct handling of worker seeding, per-worker reader instances, and cleanup of connections/cursors on worker termination. - **FR-24.** The framework shall support PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (and FSDP) by providing rank-aware sharding: each rank reads only its shard by default, with configurable sharding strategies (`by_row`, `by_file`, `by_partition`, `by_hash`, `round_robin`, `none`). - **FR-25.** Each dataset shall expose `set_epoch(epoch)` (and/or `__setstate__`/state-dict) so that shuffling and resharding can be made deterministic and distinct per epoch.  ### 5.5 Distributed Sharding and Determinism  - **FR-26.** Sharding shall be deterministic given `(source, split_spec, rank, world_size, epoch)`, producing a reproducible partition of records with no overlap and no omissions (verified by the test suite). - **FR-27.** A global seed shall control shuffling; the same seed with the same world size and epoch shall reproduce the same data order. - **FR-28.** Files/partitions shall be distributed across ranks in a balanced manner, and the framework shall expose per-rank record counts for verification. - **FR-29.** Support for reading a source once and broadcasting/broadcast-sharding to all ranks (e.g., small datasets) shall be provided via an explicit configuration option.  ### 5.6 Performance  - **FR-30.** Batch reads shall be supported natively by all backends (Hive fetch size, MySQL cursor fetch size, S3 range/list batching) to minimize per-record overhead. - **FR-31.** An optional bounded shuffle buffer and optional local disk cache/materialization layer shall be provided to improve throughput and reduce repeated remote reads. - **FR-32.** The framework shall expose read throughput metrics (records/sec, bytes/sec, latency percentiles) via an optional callback/logging interface. - **FR-33.** Where the backend supports it, predicate and column pushdown shall be used to reduce I/O; the framework shall not silently drop unsupported predicates but raise an explicit error when a requested predicate cannot be applied.  ### 5.7 Configuration  - **FR-34.** All sources and pipeline options shall be configurable via a declarative schema (Python dataclasses and/or YAML/JSON) covering: source type, connection parameters, credentials references, path/table patterns, format, read options, split/shard config, sampling, shuffling, caching, transformations, and batching. - **FR-35.** Secrets shall not be required to be stored inline in configuration files; the framework shall support environment-variable and external secret-provider references for credentials. - **FR-36.** Configuration validation shall occur at build time (before the first read) and shall raise a single aggregated error listing all invalid or missing fields. - **FR-37.** A resolved configuration object shall be serializable and printable (e.g., `to_dict()`/YAML dump) with secrets redacted, enabling logging of the effective configuration.  ### 5.8 Reliability and Error Handling  - **FR-38.** Transient failures (network errors, connection resets, throttling, 5xx responses) shall be retried with configurable exponential backoff and jitter, with a maximum retry count. - **FR-39.** Non-retryable errors (authentication failure, missing table/path, permission denied, malformed configuration) shall fail fast with clear messages that include the source identifier and the underlying cause. - **FR-40.** Readers shall implement proper resource cleanup (closing connections, cursors, file handles) on normal completion, exception, and worker shutdown; leaked resources shall not occur across repeated epochs. - **FR-41.** The framework shall emit structured warnings/errors for data-quality issues such as schema mismatch between inferred and actual data, truncated records, or parse failures, with a configurable policy to skip, quarantine, or abort.  ### 5.9 Observability and Logging  - **FR-42.** The framework shall integrate with the Python `logging` module and provide a consistent log format including source identifier, rank, worker id, and epoch. - **FR-43.** Optional progress reporting (records read, bytes read, ETA) shall be available via callback hooks and shall be safe to call from multiple workers (rank-0 aggregated by default).  ### 5.10 Extensibility  - **FR-44.** Third-party backends shall be registerable via a documented mechanism (decorator or `entry_points` group) without modifying framework source. - **FR-45.** A documented reference implementation of a custom backend shall be included, including a test harness, to lower the barrier for extension. - **FR-46.** The framework shall expose stable public interfaces such that internal refactoring does not break user code, enforced by semantic versioning and an API compatibility test.  ## 6. Non-Functional Requirements  - **NFR-1.** Python 3.9+ support; package shall be installable via `pip` and shall publish to PyPI. - **NFR-2.** Core framework shall depend only on `torch` and the standard library; each backend's third-party dependencies shall be optional extras (e.g., `pip install framework[hive]`, `[mysql]`, `[s3]`). - **NFR-3.** The framework shall not require a GPU and shall be usable in CPU-only environments. - **NFR-4.** Unit test coverage of ≥85% for core modules, and 100% coverage of sharding/splitting logic. - **NFR-5.** The framework shall maintain a documented minimum latency overhead per batch relative to a hand-written loader (≤10% for Parquet/CSV local reads). - **NFR-6.** All public APIs shall carry docstrings; user-facing documentation shall include quickstart, backend-specific configuration reference, distributed usage guide, and troubleshooting section. - **NFR-7.** CI shall run tests on Linux (and macOS/Windows where supported) across supported Python versions, including a distributed multi-process integration test using `torchrun`.  ## 7. Acceptance Criteria  1. A single configuration file can define a Hive table, a MySQL query, and an S3 prefix, and the same training script shall consume all three via `DataLoader` with only the configuration changing. 2. A user-written `collate_fn` and custom `torch.utils.data.Dataset` composition shall work without framework-specific code. 3. With `world_size=4` over a dataset of 1,000,000 rows, the union of shards read by all ranks contains each row exactly once, verified by an automated test. 4. Running the same configuration with the same seed twice produces byte-identical sample ordering. 5. A missing optional dependency (e.g., `pyarrow` for S3 Parquet) produces an actionable error message and does not prevent importing the framework or other backends. 6. Adding a new custom backend via the documented plugin interface requires no changes to framework core, and passes the supplied backend conformance test suite. 7. Credentials are never printed in logs or serialized configuration output.  ## 8. Deliverables  - Core package: source abstraction, reader abstraction, plugin registry, schema/type system, transformation pipeline, sharding/splitting, caching, config system, metrics/logging. - Backend plugins: `hive`, `mysql`, `s3` (with `local` filesystem support). - Public PyTorch integration API returning `Dataset`/`IterableDataset` implementations. - Configuration schema + YAML/JSON loader with validation and secret redaction. - Test suite: unit, integration (against local MySQL/Hive/MinIO test fixtures or mocks), distributed, and conformance tests for third-party backends. - Documentation: quickstart, backend guides, distributed guide, custom backend guide, troubleshooting, and an example project demonstrating end-to-end training over all supported backends.
explanation: The requirement is detailed and mostly clear, though some API specifics (e.g., exact factory function signatures) are open to interpretation, making it slightly ambiguous. It provides concrete, testable criteria and measurable performance targets, making it highly verifiable. It focuses on a single unified data reading framework, so it is singular.

requirement: ## Requirement: Zero-Allocation API Surface for the Godot C# Bindings  ### 1. Motivation  The current Godot C# bindings allocate managed memory on nearly every interaction with the engine API. Every call that returns or accepts a collection or byte buffer (`PackedByteArray`, `PackedInt32Array`, `PackedVector2Array`, `Godot.Collections.Array`, `string` conversions, `Variant` conversions) marshals the data into a freshly allocated managed array/object, and every call that takes a `Variant` boxes its argument. This makes the bindings unsuitable for allocation-sensitive workloads such as per-frame gameplay code, hot networking/serialization loops, physics callbacks, and procedural generation, where GC pressure causes frame spikes and unbounded memory growth. Developers currently have no supported way to call into Godot without allocating.  ### 2. Goal  Expose a first-class, allocation-free API in the Godot C# bindings that allows hot-path code to read from and write to engine data using caller-owned, stack-allocated, or pooled buffers, without intermediate managed allocations, boxing, or garbage-collector-visible garbage.  ### 3. In Scope  #### 3.1 Span-based data access for Packed arrays and buffers  For every packed array type (`PackedByteArray`, `PackedInt32Array`, `PackedInt64Array`, `PackedFloat32Array`, `PackedFloat64Array`, `PackedStringArray`, `PackedVector2Array`, `PackedVector3Array`, `PackedVector4Array`, `PackedColorArray`, `PackedInt32Array`, etc.) and for buffer-like engine types (e.g. image data, mesh surfaces, packet payloads, file contents), the bindings must provide:  - A `ReadOnlySpan<T>`-based accessor that returns a view directly over the engine-owned native memory when the data is contiguous and blittable, so no copy and no allocation occurs. The span must remain valid only for the duration of the enclosing call or until the underlying data is mutated/destroyed; this lifetime must be documented explicitly. - A `Span<T>`-based mutator (or an equivalent `void Fill(Span<T>)` / `void CopyTo(Span<T>)` pattern) allowing the caller to read data into a caller-supplied `stackalloc`/`ArrayPool` buffer without allocating a temporary managed array. - Constructors and setters that accept `ReadOnlySpan<T>` and copy directly into the native buffer, avoiding the temporary `T[]` allocation currently required.  #### 3.2 Non-allocating string interop  - Provide overloads that accept `ReadOnlySpan<char>` for APIs taking `String`/`StringName`, and a mechanism to obtain the engine string's UTF-8 bytes as a `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` without allocating an intermediate `string` or `byte[]`. - Provide a UTF-8 <-> managed string conversion helper that writes into caller-provided `Span<byte>`/`Span<char>` buffers.  #### 3.3 Non-boxing Variant and argument passing  - Provide strongly typed, non-boxing overloads for the most frequently used `Variant` conversions (numeric types, `bool`, `Vector2/3/4`, `Quaternion`, `Transform2D/3D`, `Color`, `StringName`, `GodotObject` references), so that hot-path calls do not box values into `Variant`. - Where a `Variant` must still be produced, provide a reusable, stack-allocatable `Variant`-like value type or a `VariantWriter`/`VariantScope` helper that allows reuse across calls without per-call allocation.  #### 3.4 Enumeration and collection iteration without allocation  - Provide span/index-based enumeration over `Godot.Collections.Array` and `Godot.Collections.Dictionary` (e.g. `int Count` + indexer/`Get` by index, `CollectionsMarshal`-style accessors) so that iterating engine collections does not allocate enumerator objects or boxed elements. - `foreach` over `Godot.Collections.Array`/`Dictionary` must not allocate.  #### 3.5 Native interop helpers  - Expose a documented, supported way to obtain a pointer/id (e.g. `IntPtr`/`nint`) to the native data of an engine object, plus safe wrapper helpers to operate on that memory without marshalling through managed arrays. These must be clearly marked as advanced/unsafe with documented lifetime and ownership rules.  ### 4. Out of Scope  - Changing the behaviour, semantics, or public shape of existing allocating APIs. Existing APIs must remain source- and binary-compatible and continue to allocate as they do today. - A wholesale replacement of `Godot.Collections` types. - Guaranteeing zero allocation for engine-side work that is inherently allocating on the engine side (e.g. creating new resources); the requirement targets managed-side garbage only. - Native (C++) API changes to the engine other than those required to expose contiguous memory and avoid copies.  ### 5. Non-Functional Requirements  - **Zero managed allocations:** The new APIs must not cause any managed heap allocation (no boxing, no temporary arrays, no `string` conversions) on the hot path. This must be verifiable via `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()` measurement in tests and via allocation profiling. - **Safety:** Span-based views over engine memory must not allow the caller to write out of bounds or to use memory after the owner is freed. The bindings must guard against use-after-free where detectable and must document the risks where they cannot. - **Consistency:** The API shape must be uniform across all packed array and buffer types (naming, ordering, nullability, documentation) so that a single pattern is learned once. - **Documentation:** Every new API must be annotated with whether it allocates, its lifetime rules, and thread-safety expectations. A dedicated "Zero-allocation / performance" section must be added to the C# API documentation. - **Compatibility:** Must target the currently supported .NET versions and must work with AOT/IL2CPP and with the standard `dotnet` build, including when `System.Runtime.InteropServices.CollectionsMarshal` is unavailable on the target runtime. - **No regression:** The bindings' generated source must remain deterministic and reproducible from the same API description, and source generator/binding generation must not materially increase build time.  ### 6. Usage Example (illustrative)  ```csharp // Before: allocates a byte[] per call. byte[] data = image.GetData();  // After: no managed allocation. ReadOnlySpan<byte> data = image.GetDataSpan(); Process(data); // stackalloc / Span-based processing  // Writing into a caller-owned buffer. Span<byte> scratch = stackalloc byte[1024]; int written = file.GetData(scratch); // returns bytes written, no allocation  // Iterating engine collections without allocation. var arr = node.GetChildren(); for (int i = 0; i < arr.Count; i++) {     Node child = arr.Get<Node>(i); // no enumerator allocation } ```  ### 7. Acceptance Criteria  1. All packed array types and all buffer/string/collection types listed in §3 expose span-based or index-based, non-allocating equivalents of their primary read/write operations. 2. A test suite exists that asserts **zero** managed bytes allocated per operation for the new APIs, measured with `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()` over repeated calls, covering read, write, string interop, collection iteration, and Variant-free argument passing. 3. Existing public API surface is unchanged; existing tests continue to pass unmodified. 4. Public documentation states, per API, whether it allocates, plus lifetime and thread-safety notes. 5. A migration/usage guide is published showing how to replace common allocating patterns (`GetData()`, `PackedByteArray` -> `byte[]`, `foreach` over `Godot.Collections.Array`, `Variant` arguments) with the new equivalents. 6. The implementation is verified on all supported .NET versions and under IL2CPP/AOT, and no reflection-based or trimming-unsafe constructs are introduced in the binding layer.
explanation: The requirement is detailed and precise, with explicit, testable acceptance criteria (e.g., zero managed allocations measured via GC APIs), making it highly unambiguous and verifiable. However, it addresses multiple distinct API features (span-based data access, string interop, non‑boxing variants, collection iteration, native pointers), so it is not a single, narrowly focused requirement, resulting in a low singularity score.

requirement: # Requirement: `compress/bzip2` — bzip2 (`.bz2`) encoder  ## 1. Summary  Add a **bzip2 compressor** to the `compress/bzip2` package. The encoder must emit standards‑compliant `.bz2` streams that:  * are decompressed correctly by the package's existing `Reader` (round‑trip), * are decompressed correctly by libbz2 (`bzip2`/`bunzip2` CLI) and other third‑party implementations, * pass libbz2's integrity check (`bzip2 -t`), * are produced in a fully streaming fashion (no buffering of the whole input).  The implementation must be pure Go, stdlib‑only (no cgo, no external module dependencies).  ## 2. Context / Motivation  `compress/bzip2` currently implements **decompression only**. Applications that need to *produce* `.bz2` data must either shell out to the `bzip2` binary or link against libbz2 via cgo. A native encoder removes both dependencies and completes the package's API surface.  ## 3. Scope  **In scope**  * A new streaming encoder API in package `compress/bzip2` (same package as the existing reader). * A complete bzip2 format encoder: RLE1 → BWT → MTF + RLE2 → multi‑table Huffman coding → block framing → stream framing. * Compression levels 1–9, mapping to bzip2 block sizes of 100 KiB … 900 KiB. * Unit tests, interoperability tests, fuzz targets and benchmarks.  **Out of scope (non‑goals)**  * Any change to the existing decoder behaviour (it must keep working unchanged). * Multi‑stream support (concatenated `.bz2` files): the encoder writes exactly **one** stream. * The deprecated "randomised block" feature: the encoder never emits it; the decoder's existing support for it must be preserved. * Native/assembly acceleration or SIMD; no specific performance target beyond "practically usable" (see §7). * New compression features beyond the bzip2 format (no zstd/lzma-style extensions, no custom framing).  ## 4. Public API  The API must follow the conventions of the package's existing `ReaderConfig`/`NewReader` and of the other `compress/*` packages.  ```go // WriterConfig configures a Writer. type WriterConfig struct { 	// Level is the compression level: 1 (fastest, smallest ratio) … 9 (best ratio). 	// Valid values are 1–9. The zero value selects the default level (9). 	Level int }  // NewWriter returns a Writer that compresses data written to it and writes // the resulting .bz2 stream to w. func NewWriter(w io.Writer, conf *WriterConfig) (*Writer, error)  type Writer struct{ … }  func (w *Writer) Write(p []byte) (int, error) func (w *Writer) Close() error func (w *Writer) Reset(w io.Writer) ```  Requirements on the API:  * `NewWriter` **must not** write anything to `w` before the first `Write`/`Close`. * `NewWriter` returns an error when `conf != nil` and `conf.Level` is outside `1..9`. `conf == nil` and `conf.Level == 0` select the default level (9). * `Write` accepts an arbitrary amount of data, compresses it into the current block, and returns `len(p)` on success. It must not retain `p` after returning. * `Write`/`Close` must surface errors from the underlying `io.Writer`; such errors are sticky and are returned by all subsequent calls. * `Close` flushes the final block, writes the end‑of‑stream marker and combined CRC, and finalises the stream. It is a no‑op returning `nil` if already closed. **The stream is incomplete until `Close` is called.** * `Reset` discards all buffered state and re‑arms the writer for a new, independent stream on `w` (a fresh stream header is written for the new stream). * The `Writer` is **not** safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines (document this).  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### 5.1 Normative reference  The bzip2 file format as implemented by **libbz2** is normative for all bit‑level details. The summary below states the elements that the implementation must get right; where a detail is not spelled out here, libbz2's `compress.c`/`decompress.c` (and the bzip2 format documentation) define it.  ### 5.2 Stream framing  * **Stream header:** the 4 bytes `'B'`, `'Z'`, `'h'`, followed by the ASCII digit `'1'`…`'9'` denoting the block size in units of 100 KiB. The digit **must** equal the configured level. * A stream consists of: header, zero or more compressed blocks, end‑of‑stream marker. * The encoder writes blocks of at most `level × 100 KiB` bytes of **original (pre‑RLE) input**. * **Empty input** produces a valid stream containing only the header and the end‑of‑stream marker (matching libbz2's output for an empty file, 14 bytes).  ### 5.3 Block encoding pipeline  For each block, the following stages must be applied **in this order**:  1. **RLE1 (first run‑length encoding).** Runs of ≥ 4 identical bytes are encoded as 4 literal bytes followed by a count byte holding `runLength - 4`; a run is limited to 255 bytes per encoded group, longer runs are split into consecutive groups. Runs shorter than 4 bytes are emitted literally. The RLE1 count bytes are part of the block's byte stream for all later stages (BWT, symbol map). 2. **BWT (Burrows–Wheeler transform).** Transform of the RLE1‑encoded block, yielding the sorted rotations and the primary index. The result must be *identical* to libbz2's transform for the same input. Must be implemented with a suffix‑array/suffix‑sort based algorithm of O(n log n) or better (an O(n²) implementation is not acceptable for 900 KiB blocks). 3. **MTF + RLE2 (move‑to‑front, then second run‑length encoding).** Apply move‑to‑front to the BWT output. Runs of MTF value 0 (i.e. repeated bytes) are encoded with the two special symbols `RUNA` (digit 1) and `RUNB` (digit 2) in bijective base 2, **least‑significant digit first** (run length = Σ dᵢ·2^(i‑1), dᵢ ∈ {1,2} in stream order). Non‑zero MTF values are emitted as literal symbols. 4. **Huffman coding.** Build between 2 and 6 Huffman tables over the block alphabet, assign one table per group of 50 symbols, and emit: number of tables (3 bits, value 2–6), number of selectors (15 bits), the MTF‑encoded selectors, the table definitions, and the Huffman‑coded symbol stream — exactly as specified by libbz2. EOB terminates the symbol stream.  ### 5.4 Alphabet and symbol map  * Alphabet size is `nInUse + 3`, where `nInUse` is the number of distinct byte values occurring in the **RLE1‑encoded** block:   * symbol `0` = `RUNA`, symbol `1` = `RUNB`,   * symbols `2 … nInUse+1` = literal MTF values `1 … nInUse`,   * symbol `nInUse+2` = `EOB`. * **Symbol map:** a 16‑bit bitmap marking which of the 16 groups of 16 byte values are used, followed by a 16‑bit bitmap for each used group. The map covers the byte values present in the RLE1‑encoded block (including RLE1 count bytes).  ### 5.5 Block framing  Each block is emitted as:  1. 48‑bit magic `0x314159265359`; 2. 32‑bit **block CRC** over the block's *original* (uncompressed, pre‑RLE1) data, using the CRC‑32/BZIP2 variant: polynomial `0x04C11DB7`, MSB‑first, init `0xFFFFFFFF`, final XOR `0xFFFFFFFF`; 3. the compressed block payload (symbol map, Huffman tables, symbol stream).  Blocks are **not** byte‑aligned: the next block header follows immediately after the previous block's payload bits.  ### 5.6 Stream termination  * 48‑bit end‑of‑stream magic `0x177245385090`; * 32‑bit **combined CRC**, initialised to 0 and updated per block as   `combined = rotateLeft32(combined, 1) XOR blockCRC`; * zero padding to the next byte boundary.  ### 5.7 Streaming behaviour  * The encoder must never buffer more than one block plus the BWT working structures; peak memory must stay bounded (≈ ≤ 10 MiB for level 9) regardless of input size. * Completed blocks are written to the underlying writer as soon as they are finished; the writer does not need to wait for `Close` to emit earlier blocks. * A `Write` spanning several block boundaries must be split across blocks correctly. * `Close` emits the final (possibly empty) partial block — but **no** block at all if no input bytes were ever written — followed by the end‑of‑stream marker.  ## 6. Non‑Functional Requirements  * **Dependencies:** standard library only; no cgo; no new entries in `go.mod`. * **Determinism:** the same input and level must always produce byte‑identical output (no map iteration order or randomness leaking into the output). * **Correctness of data handling:** `Write` must not modify the caller's slice; no data may be lost or duplicated across block boundaries; the round‑trip must be byte‑exact for binary data. * **Go conventions:** doc comments on all exported identifiers; package documentation updated to state that the package now implements compression as well as decompression; errors wrapped with `%w`; no panics on malformed input paths (the encoder's own inputs are trusted, but the package must remain safe under fuzzing of the decoder). * **Code quality:** the implementation must pass `go vet`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test -race`.  ## 7. Performance  * The BWT must not be implemented in O(n²); a suffix‑array based transform is required. * Provide `BenchmarkWriter` for representative inputs (highly compressible text, incompressible random data) at several levels. * No hard wall‑clock target is imposed, but compressing multi‑hundred‑megabyte inputs must be feasible in a single process without excessive memory growth.  ## 8. Testing & Acceptance Criteria  The change is accepted when all of the following hold:  1. **Round‑trip tests** (compress with `Writer`, decompress with the package's `Reader`) pass for at least:    * empty input; single byte; all 256 byte values;    * runs of identical bytes longer than 255 bytes (exercising RLE1 split and RLE2 bijective base‑2 coding);    * long runs of `0x00` and `0xFF` (exercising the BWT zero‑run path);    * incompressible random data;    * data of exactly one block size, one block size ± 1 byte, and several blocks (multi‑block stream);    * data written in many small `Write` calls vs. one large call (identical output). 2. **Interoperability tests** (skipped, not failed, when the external tools are unavailable):    * `bzip2 -t` accepts the produced stream and `bzip2 -d` recovers the original data;    * the package's `Reader` decompresses the output of `bzip2 -c` (including streams produced with all levels 1–9). 3. **Format tests** assert:    * the 4‑byte header is `"BZh"` + the configured level digit;    * the 48‑bit block magic and the 48‑bit end‑of‑stream magic are present at the expected bit positions;    * the combined CRC equals the value computed independently by the test;    * no block exceeds the configured block size;    * the output of an empty input is 14 bytes. 4. **Fuzz targets** are added: one that compresses arbitrary input and decompresses it back (must round‑trip), and one that feeds arbitrary bytes to the decoder (must not panic). 5. `go test -race ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; benchmarks are committed.  ## 9. Open Questions / Decisions to be Confirmed  * Level API shape: `WriterConfig{Level int}` (symmetric with the existing `ReaderConfig`) is the recommended choice; an alternative `NewWriterLevel(w, level)` helper may be added if reviewers prefer the `compress/flate` style. * Default level when `conf == nil` or `conf.Level == 0`: recommended value 9 (best ratio), consistent with the bzip2 CLI default. * Whether to add a `Flush() error` method: not required — bzip2 has no flush semantics — but the encoder must emit completed blocks eagerly so that long‑running writers make progress.

requirement: # Requirement: WebGPU Support  ## 1. Overview  Add first-class support for the WebGPU API as a rendering backend, alongside the existing rendering path(s), enabling the project to run on WebGPU-capable browsers/agents while preserving current functionality and performance on platforms where WebGPU is unavailable.  ## 2. Motivation  WebGPU is the successor to WebGL for GPU-accelerated content in the browser. Supporting it provides modern GPU features (compute shaders, storage buffers, timestamp queries, bindless resources), lower CPU overhead, and access to features unavailable in WebGL. It also future-proofs the project against deprecation of WebGL in target environments.  ## 3. Scope  ### 3.1 In Scope  - A pluggable renderer/backend abstraction that allows a WebGPU implementation to be selected at runtime. - Automatic or explicit selection of the WebGPU backend based on feature detection and user/host configuration. - A complete WebGL-equivalent rendering path implemented on top of WebGPU (all currently supported rendering features must work under WebGPU with no visual or behavioral regressions). - Graceful, deterministic fallback to the existing backend when WebGPU is unavailable, unsupported, or fails to initialize. - Configuration, build, packaging, documentation, telemetry/diagnostics, and automated test coverage.  ### 3.2 Non-Goals  - Exposing new user-visible rendering features exclusive to WebGPU in this change (beyond parity with existing features), except where required for parity. - Implementing compute-shader-based rendering pipelines or advanced GPU features not required for parity. - Removing or deprecating the existing backend. - Supporting WebGPU in environments that expose only WebGL (no behavior change there). - Native/headless GPU drivers beyond those already used by the existing backend.  ## 4. Terminology  - **Backend**: an implementation of the rendering abstraction (existing backend(s) and the new `webgpu` backend). - **Adapter**: a physical or logical GPU exposed by the WebGPU implementation (`GPUAdapter`). - **Device**: a `GPUDevice` obtained from an adapter, used for resource creation and command submission. - **Surface/Context**: the presentation target onto which the WebGPU backend renders (e.g., `GPUCanvasContext`).  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### FR-1: Backend Abstraction  The rendering code must be expressed against a backend-neutral interface. All direct WebGL/WebGPU calls must be confined to backend-specific implementations. The abstraction must support, at minimum: resource/texture creation and upload, buffer creation and update, shader/program compilation, pipeline/state creation, framebuffer/render-target binding, draw submission, and presentation.  ### FR-2: Initialization & Device Acquisition  The WebGPU backend must, on start-up:  1. Check for the presence of `navigator.gpu` and request an adapter (`requestAdapter`) with an explicit power-preference policy derived from project configuration (default: `high-performance` with fallback to `low-power`, then to any adapter). 2. Request a `GPUDevice` with only the features and limits required by the backend, using `requiredFeatures`/`requiredLimits` derived from actual usage (no blanket requests of optional features). 3. Handle `requestAdapter()` returning `null` and `requestDevice()` rejecting (including `device.lost`) as initialization failures. 4. Report initialization outcome through the project's existing initialization/status reporting mechanism, including a machine-readable reason for failure.  ### FR-3: Context & Presentation Configuration  The backend must configure the presentation context (`configure`) with an explicit `format` selected from `navigator.gpu.getPreferredCanvasFormat()` (or an explicit override), an appropriate `alphaMode`, and a usage set including at least `RENDER_ATTACHMENT`. The backend must handle canvas resize, device-pixel-ratio changes, and context reconfiguration without leaking resources or presenting stale frames.  ### FR-4: Resource Parity & Lifecycle  - Textures, buffers, and samplers created through the abstraction must behave equivalently to the existing backend, including color-space handling, premultiplied alpha, filtering, wrapping, and mipmap generation. - All GPU resources must be released deterministically via the abstraction's disposal path; no `GPUBuffer`/`GPUTexture` may be leaked across frame boundaries or on teardown. The backend must track owned resources so that backend teardown frees them all. - Missing support for a required WebGPU feature/limit must be detected at initialization and surfaced as an error rather than failing mid-frame.  ### FR-5: Shader & Pipeline Compilation  - Shaders must be authored in a form usable by both backends (e.g., WGSL with a translation step, or a shared intermediate representation), with no hand-maintained duplicate shader sets where avoidable. - Program/pipeline creation must be asynchronous-friendly: the backend must not block the main thread synchronously on `createRenderPipeline`/`createShaderModule` for more than the project's existing budget, and must expose compilation errors (including `getCompilationInfo()` messages) through the project's existing error-reporting facility. - Shader compilation errors must be surfaced with file/line information sufficient to locate the offending source.  ### FR-6: Frame Rendering  - The backend must submit work using a single command encoder per frame (or per documented batching unit), with render passes matching the existing backend's pass structure. - It must correctly handle render-target switches, clears, depth/stencil testing, blending, scissor/viewport state, and draw-call ordering. - It must implement a resource-cleanup pass (e.g., `GPUTexture.destroy()`, buffer `destroy()`) invoked according to the existing frame lifecycle. - Uncaptured errors and validation errors (`device.onuncapturederror`, error scopes) must be captured, logged with context, and surfaced to the developer-facing error overlay/console in the same manner as existing backend errors.  ### FR-7: Backend Selection & Fallback  - Selection order must be deterministic and configurable: explicit user/host setting (e.g., `?renderer=webgpu`, config option, or feature flag) → automatic detection → existing backend. - Automatic detection must select WebGPU only when `navigator.gpu` exists **and** an adapter and device are successfully obtained. - If the WebGPU backend fails at any point during initialization or during the first N frames (N configurable, default 1), the application must fall back to the existing backend transparently, re-initializing presentation state, without a page reload and without user-visible corruption. - The selected backend must be discoverable at runtime (e.g., reported in the existing debug/status overlay or exposed via a public API/property) so that users and tests can assert which backend is active. - Backend selection must be reported to the project's existing telemetry/analytics mechanism, if one exists, in compliance with its privacy policy (no new identifiers, no fingerprinting).  ### FR-8: Configuration & Build  - WebGPU support must be behind a build/runtime flag that can be disabled without code changes to the core (e.g., bundler define/environment variable plus a runtime option). - The build must not fail in environments lacking WebGPU typings/declarations; TypeScript types for WebGPU must be included and correct, with no `any`-typed escape hatches in the backend's public surface. - The bundle must not include duplicate copies of the WebGPU shader translation layer; tree-shaking must remain effective.  ### FR-9: Compatibility & Degradation Matrix  The following must be verified and documented:  | Environment | Expected behavior | |---|---| | Browser with WebGPU enabled | WebGPU backend active | | Browser without WebGPU | Existing backend active, no console errors | | Browser with WebGPU present but adapter request fails | Existing backend active, reason reported | | WebGPU device lost mid-session | Recovery attempt, then fallback to existing backend, error surfaced | | Safari / Firefox (WebGPU support status varies) | Per current support level; no crash; documented behavior |  ### FR-10: Documentation  - Document: how to enable/disable the WebGPU backend, how to force a specific backend for debugging, the support matrix, known limitations, and troubleshooting steps for common errors (e.g., "device lost", "adapter null"). - Update the project's README and/or docs site with a WebGPU section. - Any behavioral difference from the existing backend that users can observe (e.g., color/alpha handling, antialiasing, texture filtering) must be documented.  ### FR-11: Testing  - Unit tests covering backend selection logic, capability/feature detection, fallback triggers, and resource disposal bookkeeping. - Integration tests that render a deterministic reference scene under both backends and compare output against golden images with a documented, per-platform tolerance. - An automated test that runs in a WebGPU-capable environment and asserts the WebGPU backend is selected and a frame is presented successfully (skipped, not failed, when WebGPU is unavailable). - Tests must not be flaky: any timing-sensitive behavior must use deterministic synchronization (e.g., `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()`, `mapAsync`) rather than arbitrary timeouts.  ## 6. Acceptance Criteria  1. WebGPU can be enabled via configuration and, where supported by the environment, is selected automatically. 2. All features currently supported by the existing backend render correctly under WebGPU with no visual regressions beyond documented, justified differences. 3. When WebGPU is unavailable or fails to initialize, the application runs on the existing backend with no uncaught exceptions and no user-visible failure. 4. Switching/falling back mid-session does not require a reload and leaves the application in a consistent, interactive state. 5. No GPU resource leaks: repeated create/destroy cycles (≥1000 iterations) do not increase retained resource counts beyond a documented threshold, verifiable via `device` resource accounting or the browser's memory tooling. 6. Frame time and frame rate under WebGPU are not materially worse than the existing backend on the reference hardware (within an agreed margin, e.g., ≤5% median regression), or the difference is documented with justification. 7. The active backend is introspectable at runtime and covered by automated tests. 8. The WebGPU backend code passes the project's linting, type checking (strict mode, no `any` in backend public API), and code review standards. 9. Documentation listed in FR-10 is merged.  ## 7. Constraints & Assumptions  - The project targets browsers/agents with a standards-compliant WebGPU implementation; experimental or vendor-prefixed implementations are out of scope. - The existing rendering abstraction can be extended to support the parity requirements without a breaking change to the public API. - Shader sources can be shared or mechanically translated between backends; if a full translation is not feasible, maintaining parallel shader sets is acceptable provided they are generated, not hand-duplicated. - Telemetry changes are limited to reporting backend selection and must not introduce new data collection.  ## 8. Open Questions  - Should backend selection be user-facing (setting/UI) or developer-facing (URL parameter/config only)? - Is a shader translation approach (WGSL-first) in scope, or is WGSL authored directly for the WebGPU backend with GLSL retained for the existing backend? - Are compute-based features (e.g., GPU-driven transforms, image processing) desired in a follow-up milestone? - What is the acceptable visual-difference tolerance for golden-image comparison across GPU vendors and browser versions? - Is a hard requirement that WebGPU be the default when available, or opt-in for the first release?
